cards.prompt: I have three deadlines this week, but I've mapped out what to do each day.
cards.explanation: A plan turns pressure into direction — that's what makes stress helpful rather than overwhelming.

cards.prompt: I've missed dinner for four nights straight trying to catch up on deadlines.
cards.explanation: Repeatedly sacrificing basic needs like meals is a sign the load has tipped into harmful territory, not just a busy stretch.

cards.prompt: The deadline is tomorrow and I feel a jolt of urgency that's actually helping me focus.
cards.explanation: A short burst of urgency that sharpens focus is your stress response working for you — that's the helpful kind.

cards.prompt: I keep pushing the deadline back in my head because just thinking about it exhausts me.
cards.explanation: Avoidance driven by exhaustion, rather than genuine reprioritizing, is usually a sign the pressure has become overload.

cards.prompt: I'm stressed about the deadline, but honestly this is the most engaged I've felt at work in weeks.
cards.explanation: Feeling energized and engaged, even while stressed, usually means the challenge is a good match for you, not overload.

cards.prompt: I'm nervous about tomorrow's exam, but I've studied and I feel mostly ready.
cards.explanation: Nerves paired with real preparation is your body gearing up, not breaking down.

cards.prompt: I've been studying 14 hours a day and can barely remember what I read an hour ago.
cards.explanation: When effort stops producing results and just produces exhaustion, that's overload, not diligence.

cards.prompt: My hands feel shaky before the test starts, but they steady once I begin writing.
cards.explanation: Nerves that settle once you start are a normal activation response, not a sign of overload.

cards.prompt: I told myself I'd fail before even opening the exam paper.
cards.explanation: Catastrophizing before you've even started is a sign the stress has tipped into overwhelming your ability to think clearly.

cards.prompt: I feel sick to my stomach about this exam, but it's because I care about doing well, and it passes once I start.
cards.explanation: Physical nerves that fade once you engage are typical of helpful pressure — it's persistent, unrelenting distress that signals overload.

cards.prompt: I got promoted and I'm nervous, but also kind of excited to prove myself.
cards.explanation: Nervous excitement is the signature of a good challenge, not an overwhelming one.

cards.prompt: I got promoted and now I can't sleep because I'm sure I'll mess it up.
cards.explanation: When new responsibility starts eating into your sleep through fear, that's overload, not ambition.

cards.prompt: New role, new tools — I feel challenged in a good way.
cards.explanation: Feeling challenged 'in a good way' is exactly the marker of helpful pressure.

cards.prompt: I've started dreading Mondays so much I feel it in my chest by Sunday night.
cards.explanation: Physical dread building the night before is a sign the pressure has become something heavier than normal work stress.

cards.prompt: I have a lot more on my plate now, but I still look forward to logging in most mornings.
cards.explanation: Looking forward to the work, even a demanding version of it, usually means the stress is fueling you rather than draining you.

cards.prompt: I made a budget after my bills went up, and it's helping me feel in control.
cards.explanation: Taking a concrete step that restores a sense of control is the hallmark of helpful pressure.

cards.prompt: I've stopped opening my banking app because I can't handle looking at the number.
cards.explanation: Avoidance driven by dread, rather than a deliberate break, is a sign the stress has become overwhelming.

cards.prompt: Money's tight this month, but I have a plan for the next three.
cards.explanation: Having a plan even amid tightness keeps stress oriented toward action rather than panic.

cards.prompt: I lie awake doing money math in my head most nights now.
cards.explanation: When financial worry starts consistently disrupting sleep, that's a sign of overload, not normal budgeting stress.

cards.prompt: I'm anxious about the bill due Friday, but making the payment plan call actually calmed me down.
cards.explanation: Taking an action that lowers your anxiety, even a hard one, shows the stress is still moving you forward, not overwhelming you.

cards.prompt: I get butterflies before presenting, but I know my material.
cards.explanation: Butterflies with genuine preparation underneath are a classic sign of helpful pressure.

cards.prompt: I've cancelled plans with friends three weekends in a row because socializing feels like too much.
cards.explanation: Repeated withdrawal from things you'd normally enjoy is a sign stress has tipped into overload.

cards.prompt: I feel a spike of nerves walking on stage, and it usually settles by my second sentence.
cards.explanation: Nerves that resolve quickly once you're in motion are your activation response doing its job.

cards.prompt: I rehearse conversations in my head for hours before they happen, and it never feels like enough.
cards.explanation: Endless rehearsal that never feels sufficient is a sign anxiety has taken over, not just careful preparation.

cards.prompt: I get nervous meeting new people, but I still say yes to the invite.
cards.explanation: Following through despite nerves, rather than avoiding, usually means the stress hasn't taken over your decisions yet.

cards.prompt: It's a full house this week, but we have a plan for who does what.
cards.explanation: A shared plan under a heavy load keeps stress feeling manageable rather than crushing.

cards.prompt: I haven't had a moment to myself in three weeks and I'm starting to snap at everyone.
cards.explanation: Snapping under sustained lack of rest is a clear sign the load has become overload.

cards.prompt: Juggling school pickups and work calls is a lot, but it's manageable so far.
cards.explanation: 'A lot but manageable' is exactly the space where helpful pressure lives.

cards.prompt: I feel resentful of the people I'm caring for now, and then guilty for feeling that.
cards.explanation: Building resentment followed by guilt is a sign caregiving stress has become too heavy to sustain as-is.

cards.prompt: Caregiving is exhausting some days, but I still feel proud when I think about it.
cards.explanation: Feeling pride or meaning alongside the tiredness usually means you're stretched, not broken — that's a sign of sustainable, if heavy, pressure.

cards.prompt: I've got five things on my list today, but I know the order I'm tackling them in.
cards.explanation: Clarity on order, even with a full list, is what keeps a busy day feeling like helpful pressure.

cards.prompt: I keep switching between tasks so fast I can't remember what I actually finished.
cards.explanation: Losing track of your own progress is a sign the pace has outrun what you can actually process.

cards.prompt: It's a busy day, but each task feels doable one at a time.
cards.explanation: Breaking a busy day into doable pieces is a sign you're still in control of the pressure.

cards.prompt: My to-do list has tripled and I've started just staring at it instead of starting.
cards.explanation: Freezing in front of a list, rather than picking a starting point, is a sign the load has become overwhelming.

cards.prompt: I have too much on today, honestly, but ticking things off is oddly satisfying.
cards.explanation: If completing tasks still feels rewarding rather than just relieving, the load is heavy but you're still coping with it well.

cards.prompt: My shoulders are tense before the meeting, but they relax once it starts.
cards.explanation: Tension that eases once you're in motion is a normal, temporary stress response.

cards.prompt: I've had a headache every day this week and I don't remember the last full night's sleep.
cards.explanation: Persistent physical symptoms stacking up over days are a sign the stress has become overload.

cards.prompt: My heart's racing a bit, but a few deep breaths settle it down.
cards.explanation: A racing heart that responds to a few calming breaths shows your system recovering quickly, which is healthy.

cards.prompt: I've noticed my jaw hurts from clenching it all day, most days now.
cards.explanation: Chronic physical tension that's become a daily pattern is a sign of sustained overload, not a passing moment of stress.

cards.prompt: I feel a knot in my stomach before big moments, but it's gone an hour later.
cards.explanation: Physical tension that passes once the moment does is a normal stress response, not overload — overload tends to linger.

cards.prompt: I want this project to be good, so I've built in time to revise it.
cards.explanation: Planning revision time shows care that's channeled into action, which is a healthy kind of pressure.

cards.prompt: I've rewritten the same paragraph eleven times and I still can't send it.
cards.explanation: Being stuck in an endless loop with no sense of 'good enough' is a sign perfectionism has turned into overload.

cards.prompt: I care about getting this right, and that's actually kept me motivated all week.
cards.explanation: Care that fuels motivation, rather than paralysis, is the helpful side of high standards.

cards.prompt: Nothing I do feels finished enough, so I keep delaying handing anything in.
cards.explanation: Chronic delay driven by never feeling 'finished enough' is a sign the standard has become unreachable and draining.

cards.prompt: I redid the slide three times, but each version genuinely got better.
cards.explanation: Revising because it's improving the work is healthy drive — it becomes overload when the revising is driven by fear rather than progress.

cards.prompt: It was an intense week, but I took the weekend fully off and feel recharged.
cards.explanation: Being able to recharge after an intense stretch is a sign the pressure was sustainable.

cards.prompt: It's been an intense month and even my days off don't feel like a break anymore.
cards.explanation: When rest stops actually restoring you, that's a strong sign of overload, not just a hard month.

cards.prompt: I pushed hard this week, and I can already feel my energy coming back today.
cards.explanation: Energy bouncing back after a hard push shows your system recovering the way it's meant to.

cards.prompt: I don't remember the last time I felt actually rested, even after sleeping in.
cards.explanation: Rest that no longer restores you, even with enough sleep, is a sign the load has outpaced your recovery.

cards.prompt: I'm still tired from this week, but I'm looking forward to next week anyway.
cards.explanation: Tiredness paired with genuine anticipation for what's next usually signals you've recovered enough — chronic dread, not tiredness, is the marker of overload.

cards.prompt: I jumped when the door slammed, then laughed it off a second later.
cards.explanation: A quick startle that resolves on its own is a normal, healthy nervous system response.

cards.prompt: My body still tenses up walking into any room that reminds me of it.
cards.explanation: A persistent, widespread physical reaction to reminders is a sign that extra support could help.

cards.prompt: A loud noise startled me, and my heart raced for a minute before it passed.
cards.explanation: A brief racing heart that settles within minutes is a typical stress response, not a red flag.

cards.prompt: I've started avoiding entire streets because they resemble where it happened.
cards.explanation: Avoidance that keeps expanding to more and more places is a sign the reaction is affecting daily life.

cards.prompt: I flinched at the sound, and felt shaky for the rest of the afternoon before it faded by evening.
cards.explanation: A startle response that gradually fades over hours is still within normal range — it's when it doesn't fade, or worsens, that support helps.

cards.prompt: The date came around and I felt a wave of sadness, then it passed by evening.
cards.explanation: A wave of feeling tied to a meaningful date, that passes on its own, is a normal part of processing.

cards.prompt: Every year around that date, I can't function for days beforehand.
cards.explanation: A recurring, disabling reaction each year is a sign it may help to have extra support around that time.

cards.prompt: Seeing something that reminded me of it gave me a jolt, but I kept going with my day.
cards.explanation: A jolt that doesn't derail your day shows you're able to move through the reminder.

cards.prompt: I've had to leave work early every time a reminder comes up, for months now.
cards.explanation: A consistent pattern of being unable to function around reminders, over months, is worth bringing to a professional.

cards.prompt: The anniversary hit harder this year than last, but I still made it through the day.
cards.explanation: Some years feeling harder than others is normal — what matters more is whether you can still function, not whether the feeling is completely gone.

cards.prompt: I had one rough night after thinking about it, then slept fine the next few nights.
cards.explanation: A single rough night followed by a return to normal sleep is a typical, non-concerning pattern.

cards.prompt: I haven't slept through a full night in months because of the nightmares.
cards.explanation: Months of disrupted sleep from nightmares is a sign it's worth getting support.

cards.prompt: I woke up once startled from a dream about it, then fell back asleep.
cards.explanation: An isolated disturbed night that resolves quickly is well within the range of normal processing.

cards.prompt: I've started staying awake on purpose to avoid the dreams.
cards.explanation: Actively avoiding sleep to escape dreams is a sign the impact has grown large enough to need support.

cards.prompt: I still get the occasional bad dream about it, months later, but they're rarer than they used to be.
cards.explanation: Occasional dreams that are becoming less frequent over time is the normal shape of processing — support helps when things are getting more frequent or intense instead.

cards.prompt: I skipped watching a show with a similar scene, just wasn't in the mood that night.
cards.explanation: Choosing not to engage with something in the moment is a normal, mild form of self-protection.

cards.prompt: I've quietly dropped every friend who knew about what happened.
cards.explanation: Cutting off your entire support network is a sign the avoidance has grown large enough to need attention.

cards.prompt: I changed the subject when it came up at dinner, then joined back into the conversation.
cards.explanation: Briefly steering away from a hard topic while staying present is a normal coping move.

cards.prompt: I've stopped leaving the house except for work, for the past two months.
cards.explanation: A sustained shrinking of your world over months is a sign the avoidance needs more support than you can give it alone.

cards.prompt: I still avoid one specific thing that reminds me of it, but everything else in my life feels normal.
cards.explanation: One specific, contained avoidance while the rest of life keeps functioning is common — it becomes a bigger concern when avoidance keeps spreading to more areas.

cards.prompt: I cried thinking about it out of nowhere, and felt lighter afterward.
cards.explanation: An unexpected wave of emotion that leaves you feeling lighter is a healthy sign of release.

cards.prompt: I feel numb about it most days, like I can't access any feeling at all anymore.
cards.explanation: Persistent emotional numbness is a sign that support could help you reconnect safely.

cards.prompt: It hit me randomly in the grocery store, I teared up, then finished shopping.
cards.explanation: A brief wave that doesn't stop you from continuing your day is a normal part of processing.

cards.prompt: I feel like I'm either completely fine or completely overwhelmed, with nothing in between.
cards.explanation: Swinging only between two extremes, with no middle ground, is a sign support could help you find steadier footing.

cards.prompt: I felt a wave of grief about it during a quiet moment, and let myself sit with it before moving on.
cards.explanation: Letting a wave come and pass, staying present through it, is a healthy sign of processing — it's when waves take over entirely, or get blocked out completely, that support helps.

cards.prompt: I was a little more guarded with a new person at first, then warmed up over time.
cards.explanation: Warming up gradually, after initial caution, is a normal way trust rebuilds.

cards.prompt: I've decided I can't trust anyone again because of what happened.
cards.explanation: A blanket, permanent shutdown of trust is a sign it could help to process this with support.

cards.prompt: I needed reassurance from my partner this week more than usual, and it helped.
cards.explanation: Needing and receiving reassurance, and having it help, is a healthy way of leaning on support.

cards.prompt: I've started pushing away everyone who tries to get close, even people who've shown up for me.
cards.explanation: Pushing away people who've proven trustworthy is a sign the guardedness has become self-isolating.

cards.prompt: I still get a flicker of doubt in new relationships, but I let people in anyway.
cards.explanation: A flicker of doubt that doesn't stop you from connecting is normal caution, not a red flag — it's the shutting-everyone-out pattern that's worth addressing.

cards.prompt: Some details of that day are fuzzy, but I remember the important parts clearly.
cards.explanation: Some fuzziness in memory is completely normal, especially for difficult events.

cards.prompt: I have entire days I can't account for around that time, and it worries me.
cards.explanation: Losing entire stretches of time, in a way that worries you, is worth exploring with a professional.

cards.prompt: It comes back to me in pieces sometimes, more clearly on some days than others.
cards.explanation: Memory that varies in clarity day to day is a typical way memory works, not a warning sign.

cards.prompt: I get flashbacks so vivid I lose track of where I actually am.
cards.explanation: Losing your grip on the present moment during a flashback is a sign support could help.

cards.prompt: My memory of it feels different depending on my mood that day, but the core facts stay the same.
cards.explanation: Emotional coloring changing while the facts stay consistent is typical of how memory works — losing time or place, rather than detail, is the bigger signal.

cards.prompt: It was a hard week emotionally, but I still got my work done.
cards.explanation: Staying functional through a hard emotional week shows resilience, not a problem.

cards.prompt: I've been calling in sick most weeks because I can't get out of bed.
cards.explanation: A recurring inability to function week after week is a sign it's time to bring in extra support.

cards.prompt: I had a rough moment mid-day, took a walk, and got back to it.
cards.explanation: Using a small break to reset and continue is a healthy coping strategy.

cards.prompt: I've stopped doing things I used to enjoy completely, for a long stretch now.
cards.explanation: A prolonged loss of interest in things you once enjoyed is a sign worth addressing with support.

cards.prompt: I'm slower at getting things done lately, but I'm still getting them done.
cards.explanation: A slower pace that still moves forward is manageable — it's a full stop on daily life, sustained over time, that's the clearer signal to reach out for support.

cards.prompt: I told a friend a little about it, and felt relieved afterward.
cards.explanation: Sharing a piece of it and feeling relief afterward is a healthy sign of processing.

cards.prompt: I've never told a single person, and the thought of it makes me panic.
cards.explanation: Panic at the mere thought of speaking about it is a sign professional support could really help.

cards.prompt: I can talk about it now more easily than I could a year ago.
cards.explanation: Increasing ease over time is a strong, healthy sign of healing.

cards.prompt: I feel like no one would believe me, so I've stopped trying to talk about it at all.
cards.explanation: Isolating around a fear of not being believed is a sign it would help to talk to someone trained to listen without judgment.

cards.prompt: Talking about it still brings up some emotion, but I don't dread the conversations anymore.
cards.explanation: Emotion surfacing without dread is a sign you've built some safety around the topic — persistent panic or isolation around it is what signals a need for more support.

cards.prompt: It's been a while, and while I still think of it, it doesn't run my day anymore.
cards.explanation: Still thinking of it while no longer having it dominate your day is a sign of healthy processing over time.

cards.prompt: It's been years, and it still feels as raw as day one.
cards.explanation: No softening at all over years is a sign it could help to process this with support.

cards.prompt: I have good stretches and hard stretches, but the good stretches are getting longer.
cards.explanation: A gradually improving ratio of good to hard stretches is exactly what healthy healing looks like.

cards.prompt: Nothing about how it feels has changed, no matter how much time passes.
cards.explanation: A total lack of change over a long time is a sign it's worth getting outside support.

cards.prompt: I thought I was 'over it,' then it resurfaced this year — but I got through it faster this time.
cards.explanation: Resurfacing occasionally is part of normal healing, especially if each time it's a little easier to move through — it's when nothing ever seems to ease that reaching out helps.

cards.prompt: I said no to a task that wasn't mine to do.
cards.explanation: Saying no to what isn't yours is exactly how sustainable drive protects itself.

cards.prompt: I say yes to everything because I'm scared of how it'll look if I don't.
cards.explanation: Saying yes out of fear rather than choice is a classic early sign of burnout building.

cards.prompt: I set my hours and mostly stick to them.
cards.explanation: Sticking to your own hours most of the time shows a boundary that's actually holding.

cards.prompt: I answer work messages the second they come in, even at midnight.
cards.explanation: Being 'on' at all hours with no real off-switch is a strong sign of burnout patterns.

cards.prompt: I made an exception to help on an urgent thing this week, but it's rare for me.
cards.explanation: One reasonable exception doesn't undo a healthy boundary — burnout is about the exception becoming the norm.

cards.prompt: I took my lunch break away from my desk today.
cards.explanation: Stepping away for lunch is a small but real sign your work rhythm still has breathing room.

cards.prompt: I eat lunch at my desk while still answering emails, most days.
cards.explanation: A daily habit of never fully stepping away is a sign the pace has become unsustainable.

cards.prompt: I logged off on time and it actually felt fine.
cards.explanation: Logging off without guilt is a sign your relationship with work is currently healthy.

cards.prompt: I feel guilty the moment I stop working, even for five minutes.
cards.explanation: Guilt attached to any pause, however small, is a hallmark of burnout thinking.

cards.prompt: I took a short break today, but I still thought about work the whole time.
cards.explanation: Taking the break at all is a good sign, even if your mind wandered — burnout looks more like being unable to step away in the first place.

cards.prompt: I told my manager I was overloaded and we adjusted my workload.
cards.explanation: Speaking up and getting a real adjustment is sustainable drive working exactly as it should.

cards.prompt: I keep saying 'I'm fine' when asked, even though I'm not.
cards.explanation: Habitually masking how you actually feel is a sign burnout is building beneath the surface.

cards.prompt: I asked a coworker for help on a task instead of struggling alone.
cards.explanation: Asking for help when you need it is a healthy, sustainable way of managing your load.

cards.prompt: I've stopped speaking up in meetings because it feels pointless now.
cards.explanation: Going quiet out of a sense of futility is a common burnout pattern.

cards.prompt: I raised a concern about my workload and it didn't fully get resolved, but I said it anyway.
cards.explanation: Speaking up, even if the outcome isn't perfect, keeps you engaged — burnout tends to show up as going quiet altogether.

cards.prompt: My plate is full this month, but I know it'll ease up next month.
cards.explanation: Seeing an end in sight helps a heavy month feel like a phase, not a permanent state.

cards.prompt: Every month feels like the busiest month, with no end in sight.
cards.explanation: A permanent sense of 'no end in sight' is a strong signal of burnout, not just a busy season.

cards.prompt: I have a lot to do, but I'm prioritizing what matters most.
cards.explanation: Being able to prioritize under load is a sign you still feel some control over your work.

cards.prompt: Everything feels equally urgent all the time, so I don't know where to start.
cards.explanation: Losing the ability to tell what's actually urgent is a common effect of chronic overload.

cards.prompt: I'm behind on a few things this week, but I have a plan to catch up.
cards.explanation: Being behind with a plan is normal work pressure — burnout is being behind with no sense that catching up is even possible.

cards.prompt: I still feel some pull toward the parts of my job I actually enjoy.
cards.explanation: Still feeling drawn to parts of your work is a strong sign of sustainable engagement.

cards.prompt: I feel completely indifferent to my work now, even the parts I used to like.
cards.explanation: Losing interest even in the parts you used to enjoy is a hallmark sign of burnout.

cards.prompt: I had a good day at work today and it reminded me why I like this job.
cards.explanation: Being reminded why you like your job, even occasionally, is a sign the connection to it is still alive.

cards.prompt: I can't remember the last time I felt anything but tired about work.
cards.explanation: A long stretch with no positive feeling toward work at all is a strong burnout signal.

cards.prompt: I'm not thrilled about work this week, but I know that's just this week.
cards.explanation: A low week that you can place in context is normal — burnout tends to feel like every week, indefinitely.

cards.prompt: I got positive feedback and let myself feel good about it.
cards.explanation: Being able to take in positive feedback shows you're still emotionally connected to your work.

cards.prompt: Nothing feels like it's ever enough, no matter what feedback I get.
cards.explanation: Feeling like nothing is ever enough, regardless of the feedback, is a common burnout thought pattern.

cards.prompt: I noticed my own progress on a project today.
cards.explanation: Being able to notice your own progress is a healthy, sustaining habit.

cards.prompt: I feel invisible at work no matter what I accomplish.
cards.explanation: A persistent sense of invisibility regardless of achievement is a sign of burnout, not just modesty.

cards.prompt: I got praised today but brushed it off quickly — that's just how I am.
cards.explanation: Brushing off praise out of habit is common and not itself a red flag — burnout shows up more as feeling numb to any recognition at all, not just modest about it.

cards.prompt: I noticed a coworker's success and felt a little inspired.
cards.explanation: Feeling inspired by someone else's success is a sign your own motivation is still intact.

cards.prompt: I compare myself to everyone and always come up short, constantly.
cards.explanation: Constant unfavorable comparison is a common symptom of burnout eating into self-worth.

cards.prompt: Someone got a promotion and I was genuinely happy for them.
cards.explanation: Genuine happiness for others' success is a sign you're not running on empty.

cards.prompt: I resent everyone around me lately, even people I used to like.
cards.explanation: Widespread resentment, even toward people you liked, is a sign burnout is affecting how you see everyone.

cards.prompt: I felt a flicker of envy seeing a coworker's win, but it passed.
cards.explanation: A brief flicker of envy is a normal human reaction — ongoing resentment that colors how you see everyone is more of a burnout signal.

cards.prompt: I feel a bit tired by Friday, but weekends restore me.
cards.explanation: Weekly tiredness that recovers over the weekend is a normal, sustainable rhythm.

cards.prompt: I feel exhausted even after a full weekend off.
cards.explanation: Exhaustion that survives a full weekend of rest is a strong sign of burnout.

cards.prompt: I get a normal headache after a long day sometimes.
cards.explanation: An occasional headache after a hard day is a normal physical response, not a warning sign.

cards.prompt: I've had constant headaches and stomach issues for weeks now.
cards.explanation: Weeks of ongoing physical symptoms is a sign the stress has become chronic overload.

cards.prompt: I'm more tired than usual this week, but I can still tell it's temporary.
cards.explanation: Recognizing tiredness as temporary usually means you're still tracking your own state accurately — burnout often removes that sense of 'this will pass.'

cards.prompt: I mostly unplug on weekends and come back Monday feeling okay.
cards.explanation: Unplugging and returning to work feeling okay is a sign your rhythm is currently sustainable.

cards.prompt: I spend my weekends dreading Monday instead of resting.
cards.explanation: Weekends consumed by dread instead of rest is a sign work stress has taken over your recovery time.

cards.prompt: I checked email once this weekend, then put my phone away.
cards.explanation: Checking briefly and then stepping back shows you still have some control over the habit.

cards.prompt: I can't remember my last weekend that felt like an actual break.
cards.explanation: A long stretch with no real breaks is a strong burnout signal.

cards.prompt: I did a bit of work on Sunday, but it was by choice, not pressure.
cards.explanation: Choosing to do a little work isn't the same as feeling unable to stop — burnout is marked by the compulsion, not the occasional voluntary hour.

cards.prompt: I can picture myself doing this job a year from now, mostly content.
cards.explanation: Being able to picture a mostly content future in this job is a sign of sustainable drive.

cards.prompt: I can't imagine doing this job for even another month.
cards.explanation: A sense that you can't even imagine continuing is a strong burnout signal worth taking seriously.

cards.prompt: There are hard days, but overall I still feel like this job fits me.
cards.explanation: An overall sense of fit, even with hard days, points to a sustainable relationship with your work.

cards.prompt: I fantasize about quitting almost every single day now.
cards.explanation: A daily fantasy of quitting is a common and serious sign of burnout.

cards.prompt: I've thought about quitting a few times this year, but each time it passed.
cards.explanation: The thought crossing your mind occasionally is common — it's when the thought becomes a daily, unshakable pull that it signals burnout rather than a passing rough patch.

cards.prompt: I went for a 10-minute walk even though I didn't feel like it.
cards.explanation: Showing up for a small version of the habit, even without motivation, is exactly how habits get built.

cards.prompt: I skipped the gym again and told myself I'll 'start Monday.'
cards.explanation: Repeatedly pushing the start date is a quiet way of avoiding the habit altogether.

cards.prompt: I did a short stretch session instead of my full workout, and that was enough today.
cards.explanation: Scaling down without skipping entirely keeps the habit alive.

cards.prompt: I keep planning workouts I know I won't actually do.
cards.explanation: Planning without any real intention to follow through is a subtle form of self-sabotage.

cards.prompt: I only did half my usual workout today, but I still showed up.
cards.explanation: Showing up in a smaller way still counts as building the habit — self-sabotage looks more like the pattern of planning and then not showing up at all.

cards.prompt: I had a good breakfast and felt fueled for the morning.
cards.explanation: Eating in a way that fuels you is a straightforward sign of building a good habit.

cards.prompt: I skipped a meal to 'make up for' eating out yesterday.
cards.explanation: Skipping meals to compensate for a previous one is a quiet, unhealthy pattern rather than a fix.

cards.prompt: I had dessert and didn't spiral about it afterward.
cards.explanation: Enjoying something without spiraling shows a settled, sustainable relationship with food.

cards.prompt: I told myself I'd 'be good' tomorrow so it's fine to skip eating properly today.
cards.explanation: Using a future promise to justify neglecting yourself today is a self-sabotage pattern.

cards.prompt: I ate more than planned at dinner, but I just moved on and had a normal breakfast the next day.
cards.explanation: Moving on without compensating afterward is what a stable relationship with food looks like — the compensating pattern is the sabotage, not the occasional bigger meal.

cards.prompt: I went to bed at a consistent time again tonight.
cards.explanation: Consistency at bedtime is one of the simplest and most powerful habit-building moves.

cards.prompt: I keep telling myself 'just one more episode' until it's 2am, most nights.
cards.explanation: A repeated pattern of overriding your own need for sleep is a quiet form of self-sabotage.

cards.prompt: I put my phone away earlier to wind down before bed.
cards.explanation: A small, deliberate change to support better sleep is exactly how habits get built.

cards.prompt: I know I need sleep, but I scroll anyway most nights, on purpose.
cards.explanation: Knowingly working against your own needs, night after night, is a self-sabotage pattern.

cards.prompt: I stayed up a bit late last night, but I still got up at my normal time today.
cards.explanation: One late night that doesn't derail your routine is normal life — the sabotage pattern is repeatedly choosing the late night over the thing you know you need.

cards.prompt: I noticed I skipped a workout and just planned for tomorrow instead.
cards.explanation: Noticing a miss and moving forward without drama is exactly how sustainable habits survive slip-ups.

cards.prompt: I skipped one workout and decided the whole week is 'ruined' anyway.
cards.explanation: Letting one miss spiral into giving up on the whole week is a self-sabotage pattern.

cards.prompt: I had an off day and didn't let it spiral into giving up.
cards.explanation: Keeping an off day contained, rather than letting it define the whole effort, is what building a habit actually looks like.

cards.prompt: I use one slip-up as an excuse to abandon the whole plan.
cards.explanation: Treating a single slip as permission to quit entirely is a quiet form of self-sabotage.

cards.prompt: I was a bit hard on myself about a slip today, but I still followed through the next day.
cards.explanation: Following through despite some self-criticism is still building the habit — sabotage is when the self-criticism becomes the reason to quit entirely.

cards.prompt: I missed a few days of my routine, then just picked it back up.
cards.explanation: Picking a routine back up after missing it is the core skill of building any lasting habit.

cards.prompt: I missed a few days and used it as proof the whole thing was pointless.
cards.explanation: Using a missed stretch as 'proof' to quit is a common self-sabotage pattern.

cards.prompt: I had a setback, felt annoyed, and got back on track the next day.
cards.explanation: Feeling annoyed but still returning to the routine is a sign the habit is genuinely taking hold.

cards.prompt: One setback and I quietly abandon the entire plan, every time.
cards.explanation: A repeating pattern of total abandonment after any setback is a clear self-sabotage cycle.

cards.prompt: I had a rough week and didn't do much, but I didn't beat myself up or quit either.
cards.explanation: Staying neutral about a rough week — not spiraling, not quitting — is exactly what keeps a habit sustainable long-term.

cards.prompt: I drank water before reaching for coffee this morning.
cards.explanation: A small, deliberate swap like this is exactly how sustainable habits get built one choice at a time.

cards.prompt: I run on caffeine and barely drink water most days, and I know it.
cards.explanation: Knowingly neglecting a basic need, day after day, is a quiet self-sabotage pattern.

cards.prompt: I packed a snack so I wouldn't skip eating during a busy day.
cards.explanation: Planning ahead to meet your own needs is a clear building-habit move.

cards.prompt: I let myself get so busy I forget to eat, and secretly feel proud of it.
cards.explanation: Taking pride in neglecting a basic need is a subtle but real form of self-sabotage.

cards.prompt: I forgot to drink water for most of the day, but I caught it in the evening and had some.
cards.explanation: Catching it and course-correcting, even late, is what building a habit looks like — sabotage is not noticing at all, or noticing and not caring.

cards.prompt: I set a time to put my phone down before bed and mostly followed it.
cards.explanation: Mostly following through on a self-set limit is a strong sign of a habit taking hold.

cards.prompt: I tell myself I'll cut down on scrolling 'starting tomorrow,' every day.
cards.explanation: A daily promise that never actually starts is a familiar self-sabotage loop.

cards.prompt: I noticed I was scrolling too much and took a short break from my phone.
cards.explanation: Noticing and adjusting in the moment is exactly how healthy habits get reinforced.

cards.prompt: I know screens are wrecking my sleep, and I keep doing it anyway on purpose.
cards.explanation: Knowingly acting against your own well-being, repeatedly, is a self-sabotage pattern.

cards.prompt: I went over my screen time goal today, but I'm not going to let that stop me from trying again tomorrow.
cards.explanation: Trying again after going over is the habit-building mindset — sabotage is using today's slip as an excuse to give up on the goal altogether.

cards.prompt: I decided to skip a drink at the get-together tonight.
cards.explanation: Choosing to skip in the moment shows you're actively steering the habit, not just drifting.

cards.prompt: I keep telling myself I 'deserve' to overdo it because of a hard week, and I do it a lot.
cards.explanation: Using a hard week as a repeated justification is a quiet self-sabotage pattern.

cards.prompt: I noticed I was using a drink to cope with stress and cut back.
cards.explanation: Noticing a coping pattern and adjusting it yourself is a strong, healthy sign.

cards.prompt: I use it most nights now to unwind and don't really question it anymore.
cards.explanation: A nightly habit that's stopped being questioned is a sign it may be worth a closer look.

cards.prompt: I had more than I planned to at one event, but it's not something I do regularly.
cards.explanation: A one-off exception isn't sabotage — the concerning pattern is when it becomes the regular, unquestioned way of coping.

cards.prompt: I booked the check-up I'd been putting off.
cards.explanation: Following through on a check-up, even a delayed one, is a strong building-habit move.

cards.prompt: I've been ignoring a symptom for months because I don't want to know.
cards.explanation: Avoiding a known symptom out of fear is a form of self-sabotage worth gently interrupting.

cards.prompt: I followed up on the doctor's advice from last time.
cards.explanation: Following through on advice you've already received is a clear sign of building a healthy habit.

cards.prompt: I keep canceling appointments I actually need.
cards.explanation: A repeated pattern of cancelling needed appointments is a quiet self-sabotage pattern.

cards.prompt: I was nervous about the appointment, but I went anyway.
cards.explanation: Following through despite nerves is still taking care of yourself — the sabotage is avoiding the appointment altogether out of fear.

cards.prompt: I don't feel amazing today, but I still did my small routine.
cards.explanation: Doing the small version even without full motivation is exactly how sustainable habits are built.

cards.prompt: I only 'count' it if I feel 100% motivated, so most days don't count.
cards.explanation: Setting an all-or-nothing bar for motivation quietly guarantees most days will 'fail.'

cards.prompt: I'm doing this for how it makes me feel, not to punish myself.
cards.explanation: A motivation rooted in how it makes you feel is a sustainable foundation for a habit.

cards.prompt: I only do healthy things when I'm mad at myself about something.
cards.explanation: Using self-criticism as the only fuel for healthy behavior is a self-sabotaging cycle in disguise.

cards.prompt: My motivation is low this week, but I'm still showing up in smaller ways.
cards.explanation: Scaling down without stopping is exactly how sustainable habits survive low-motivation weeks — sabotage is treating low motivation as a reason to stop entirely.

cards.prompt: They tell me when something's bothering them instead of going quiet.
cards.explanation: Direct communication, rather than silence, is a hallmark of a healthy dynamic.

cards.prompt: They give me the silent treatment when they're upset instead of talking.
cards.explanation: Using silence as a weapon rather than talking things through is a common red flag pattern.

cards.prompt: We can disagree and still text normally an hour later.
cards.explanation: Recovering quickly from disagreement shows the relationship can handle conflict without lasting damage.

cards.prompt: They bring up things I did wrong from months ago, in every argument.
cards.explanation: Stockpiling old grievances to use in every argument is a red flag pattern, not healthy conflict.

cards.prompt: They needed a bit of space before talking about something hard, but they came back to it.
cards.explanation: Needing a short pause before a hard conversation is healthy self-regulation — the red flag is using silence as punishment instead of space.

cards.prompt: They tell me where they're going, not because I ask, but because they want to share their day.
cards.explanation: Voluntary openness, rather than obligation, is a sign of genuine trust and closeness.

cards.prompt: They check my phone or messages without asking.
cards.explanation: Checking someone's phone without consent is a clear red flag around trust and boundaries.

cards.prompt: I feel comfortable being honest with them, even about small things.
cards.explanation: Comfort with small honesty is often the clearest sign of a safe relationship.

cards.prompt: I've started hiding small things from them to avoid a reaction.
cards.explanation: Hiding small things out of fear of their reaction is a sign the relationship doesn't feel safe.

cards.prompt: I felt a flicker of jealousy seeing them with a friend, but I didn't act on it.
cards.explanation: Noticing a feeling without acting on it is normal — the red flag is when jealousy turns into control, checking, or accusations.

cards.prompt: They apologize when they're wrong, even mid-argument.
cards.explanation: The ability to apologize mid-conflict is a strong sign of emotional maturity in the relationship.

cards.prompt: They never actually apologize, they just stop talking until I do.
cards.explanation: Withholding communication until you apologize first is a manipulative red flag pattern.

cards.prompt: We can raise our voices sometimes and still repair things after.
cards.explanation: Being able to repair after a heated moment matters more than never raising your voice at all.

cards.prompt: Arguments always end with me apologizing, even when I didn't do anything.
cards.explanation: A one-sided pattern where you always end up apologizing is a red flag worth noticing.

cards.prompt: We had a real disagreement this week, but we both listened to each other's side.
cards.explanation: Mutual listening during conflict, even heated conflict, is a sign the relationship can handle disagreement — one-sided blame is the red flag.

cards.prompt: They're happy when I make plans with my own friends.
cards.explanation: Genuine support for your independence is a strong healthy sign.

cards.prompt: They get upset every time I make plans without them.
cards.explanation: Consistent upset over your independent plans is a red flag around control.

cards.prompt: We have separate hobbies and that feels normal to both of us.
cards.explanation: Comfortable separateness alongside togetherness is a sign of a healthy dynamic.

cards.prompt: They've slowly gotten me to drop hobbies and friends I used to have.
cards.explanation: A gradual shrinking of your world to fit them is a classic red flag pattern.

cards.prompt: They said they missed me while I was out with friends, and I liked hearing that.
cards.explanation: Missing you is a normal, warm feeling — the red flag is when that feeling turns into guilt-tripping or discouraging you from going.

cards.prompt: They show up for me on a hard day without me having to ask.
cards.explanation: Proactive support on hard days is a clear healthy sign.

cards.prompt: They make my hard days about how it's affecting them instead.
cards.explanation: Redirecting your hard moments back onto themselves is a red flag around emotional support.

cards.prompt: I feel like I can have a bad day around them.
cards.explanation: Feeling safe enough to have a bad day is a strong sign of a healthy, accepting relationship.

cards.prompt: I feel like I have to perform being okay around them, always.
cards.explanation: Feeling pressure to always seem fine is a sign the relationship doesn't feel emotionally safe.

cards.prompt: They were a little distracted when I told them about a bad day, but circled back later to check in.
cards.explanation: Circling back shows they still care even if the first response wasn't perfect — the red flag is a pattern of never following up at all.

cards.prompt: I deleted our old photos when I felt ready to.
cards.explanation: Letting go at your own pace, when you feel ready, is a healthy part of moving on.

cards.prompt: I've kept every message just to re-read them at 2am.
cards.explanation: Regularly re-reading old messages late at night is a sign of staying stuck rather than processing.

cards.prompt: I unfollowed them because it made moving on easier.
cards.explanation: Making an active choice to protect your own healing is a healthy sign.

cards.prompt: I check their social media multiple times a day.
cards.explanation: Frequent checking is a common pattern that keeps the wound open rather than letting it close.

cards.prompt: I still have a few of our old photos saved, but I don't look at them anymore.
cards.explanation: Keeping something without revisiting it isn't the same as holding on — it's the active re-checking and re-reading that keeps the wound open.

cards.prompt: I let myself feel sad about it today, and then went about my day.
cards.explanation: Letting sadness pass through you, rather than fighting it, is a healthy part of moving on.

cards.prompt: I've built my whole day around avoiding anything that reminds me of them.
cards.explanation: Restructuring your whole life around avoidance is a sign of staying stuck, not healing.

cards.prompt: I told a friend how I'm actually doing instead of pretending I'm fine.
cards.explanation: Being honest about how you're doing, instead of masking it, supports genuine healing.

cards.prompt: I've convinced myself I'm 'totally over it' while still checking if they've moved on.
cards.explanation: Claiming to be over it while still monitoring them is a sign you haven't actually let go yet.

cards.prompt: I thought about texting them today, and then didn't.
cards.explanation: Noticing the urge and choosing not to act on it is exactly what moving on looks like — the concerning pattern is acting on the urge repeatedly.

cards.prompt: They support my goals even when they don't fully understand them.
cards.explanation: Supporting you even without full understanding is a strong sign of respect.

cards.prompt: They make jokes about my flaws in front of friends.
cards.explanation: Public jokes at your expense, especially about sensitive things, is a red flag around respect.

cards.prompt: They ask before making plans that affect both of us.
cards.explanation: Checking in before decisions that affect you both is a basic, healthy sign of respect.

cards.prompt: They make decisions for both of us without asking me.
cards.explanation: Making unilateral decisions that affect you is a red flag around respect and equality.

cards.prompt: They teased me a little about something, and I laughed along and it didn't bother me.
cards.explanation: Light teasing that genuinely lands as fun for both people is normal — it's a red flag when the teasing targets something sensitive and continues after you've said it bothers you.

cards.prompt: Their actions match what they say, most of the time.
cards.explanation: Actions matching words, consistently, is one of the clearest signs of a trustworthy partner.

cards.prompt: They say all the right things but rarely follow through.
cards.explanation: A gap between words and actions, if it's a pattern, is a red flag worth paying attention to.

cards.prompt: I know generally what to expect from them day to day.
cards.explanation: Predictability in a good sense — knowing what to expect — is a sign of a stable relationship.

cards.prompt: I never know which version of them I'll get today.
cards.explanation: Not knowing which version of someone you'll get is a red flag around emotional consistency.

cards.prompt: They had an off day and were a bit short with me, but it wasn't the norm and they acknowledged it.
cards.explanation: An occasional off day that gets acknowledged is normal — the red flag is unpredictability with no accountability for it.

cards.prompt: We've both changed some habits based on things we've learned about each other.
cards.explanation: Mutual adjustment over time is a strong sign the relationship is growing in a healthy direction.

cards.prompt: Nothing ever changes no matter how many times I bring up the same issue.
cards.explanation: A total lack of change despite repeated conversations is a red flag around whether the relationship can actually grow.

cards.prompt: I feel like a better version of myself around them.
cards.explanation: Feeling like a better version of yourself is one of the clearest markers of a healthy relationship.

cards.prompt: I've started shrinking myself to avoid setting them off.
cards.explanation: Shrinking yourself to manage someone else's reactions is a significant red flag.

cards.prompt: We're still working through an old pattern, but I can see us both trying.
cards.explanation: Visible effort from both sides, even on an unresolved issue, is a healthy sign — the red flag is when the same issue never even gets acknowledged, let alone worked on.

cards.prompt: I got critical feedback and thought about what specifically I could improve.
cards.explanation: Turning feedback into a specific action is a realistic, constructive response.

cards.prompt: I got one piece of critical feedback and decided I'm bad at my job entirely.
cards.explanation: Generalizing one comment into a verdict on your whole ability is self-doubt talking, not accuracy.

cards.prompt: I noticed a mistake in my work and made a note to double-check next time.
cards.explanation: Learning a specific lesson from a mistake is a grounded, realistic response.

cards.prompt: I replay every piece of feedback I've ever gotten as proof I'm not good enough.
cards.explanation: Compiling all past feedback into one big case against yourself is self-doubt distorting the picture.

cards.prompt: The feedback stung at first, but once I calmed down I could see the useful part in it.
cards.explanation: Being able to extract the useful part after the sting fades is exactly what a realistic self-check looks like — self-doubt keeps circling the sting without ever getting to the useful part.

cards.prompt: I noticed someone doing something well and thought about what I could learn from it.
cards.explanation: Using someone else's success as a learning point is a realistic, constructive habit.

cards.prompt: I compare myself to everyone I see and always come up short.
cards.explanation: A constant, one-directional comparison that always ends badly is self-doubt, not an accurate read of reality.

cards.prompt: Someone else got recognized and I felt happy for them, genuinely.
cards.explanation: Genuine happiness for others shows your own sense of worth isn't being threatened.

cards.prompt: Every time someone else succeeds, it feels like proof of my own failure.
cards.explanation: Treating others' wins as evidence of your own failure is a distorted, self-doubting pattern.

cards.prompt: I felt a pang comparing myself to a colleague, but I didn't let it change how I saw myself overall.
cards.explanation: A passing pang that doesn't shake your overall self-view is normal — self-doubt turns that single moment into a verdict on your whole worth.

cards.prompt: I made a mistake and fixed what I could, then moved on.
cards.explanation: Fixing what's fixable and moving on is exactly how a realistic self-check handles a mistake.

cards.prompt: I made one mistake and now I'm sure everyone thinks I'm incompetent.
cards.explanation: Assuming everyone's judgment based on one mistake is self-doubt filling in details that aren't actually there.

cards.prompt: I own my mistakes without spiraling about them.
cards.explanation: Owning a mistake without spiraling shows a balanced, realistic self-view.

cards.prompt: I replay small mistakes for days, way past the point they matter.
cards.explanation: Replaying small mistakes far past their relevance is a sign self-doubt has taken over the story.

cards.prompt: I made a mistake today and felt embarrassed for a bit, but I still spoke up in the next meeting.
cards.explanation: Feeling embarrassed but still showing up afterward is a sign the mistake didn't take over your self-image — self-doubt tends to make you withdraw instead.

cards.prompt: I feel nervous starting something new, but I remind myself I've learned new things before.
cards.explanation: Drawing on your own track record to steady your nerves is a realistic, grounded approach.

cards.prompt: I assume I'll fail at anything new before I've even tried.
cards.explanation: Assuming failure before trying is self-doubt speaking, not an actual prediction based on evidence.

cards.prompt: I asked questions in a new setting instead of pretending to already know.
cards.explanation: Asking questions rather than pretending is a confident, realistic way to handle not knowing something yet.

cards.prompt: I stay quiet in new settings because I'm sure my questions will sound stupid.
cards.explanation: Assuming your questions will sound stupid, without evidence, is self-doubt shaping your behavior.

cards.prompt: I felt like an outsider on my first day somewhere new, but I gave it more than one day before judging it.
cards.explanation: Giving something time before judging yourself is a realistic, grounded response — self-doubt jumps straight to a verdict on day one.

cards.prompt: I made a decision, and even if it's not perfect, I trust I can adjust.
cards.explanation: Trusting your ability to adjust later is a realistic, confidence-supporting mindset.

cards.prompt: I can't make small decisions because I'm sure I'll choose wrong.
cards.explanation: Freezing over small decisions from a certainty of being wrong is self-doubt distorting the stakes.

cards.prompt: I picked an option and moved forward without endless second-guessing.
cards.explanation: Being able to commit to a choice and move on is a sign of a realistic, steady self-view.

cards.prompt: I ask everyone around me to make decisions for me because I don't trust my own judgment at all.
cards.explanation: A total lack of trust in your own judgment, across all decisions, is self-doubt rather than an accurate assessment.

cards.prompt: I went back and forth on a decision for a bit, but I still picked something and moved on.
cards.explanation: Some deliberation before deciding is completely normal — self-doubt is the version where you can't ever land on a choice, or trust the one you made.

cards.prompt: I shared my opinion in a meeting, even though I was a little nervous.
cards.explanation: Sharing your opinion despite nerves is a sign your self-doubt isn't running the show.

cards.prompt: I stay silent in meetings because I assume my ideas aren't worth sharing.
cards.explanation: Assuming your ideas aren't worth sharing, without testing that assumption, is self-doubt talking.

cards.prompt: I asked a clarifying question instead of pretending I understood.
cards.explanation: Asking for clarity rather than faking understanding is a grounded, confident move.

cards.prompt: I nod along even when I'm confused because I don't want to look dumb.
cards.explanation: Hiding confusion to avoid looking dumb is a self-doubt-driven habit that can actually undermine you.

cards.prompt: I hesitated before speaking up today, but I said it anyway.
cards.explanation: Hesitating and still speaking up shows the doubt didn't win — the concerning pattern is when hesitation turns into staying silent every time.

cards.prompt: I finished something and let myself feel proud of it, briefly.
cards.explanation: Letting yourself feel proud, even briefly, is a healthy, realistic response to your own effort.

cards.prompt: I finish things and immediately move to the next thing without ever feeling proud.
cards.explanation: Never allowing yourself a moment of pride is a self-doubt pattern that denies your own effort any weight.

cards.prompt: Someone complimented my work and I said thank you and meant it.
cards.explanation: Accepting a compliment sincerely is a sign your self-view matches what others are actually seeing.

cards.prompt: Someone complimented my work and I assumed they were just being polite.
cards.explanation: Dismissing genuine praise as mere politeness is self-doubt overriding the evidence in front of you.

cards.prompt: I got praised today and felt awkward about it, but I didn't argue with them out loud.
cards.explanation: Feeling awkward but still letting the compliment land is a normal, healthy response — self-doubt actively argues against the praise, even internally.

cards.prompt: I didn't get the opportunity, so I asked for feedback to improve next time.
cards.explanation: Turning rejection into a request for feedback is a realistic, forward-moving response.

cards.prompt: I didn't get the opportunity, so I decided I'm just not good enough, period.
cards.explanation: Turning one rejection into a permanent verdict on your worth is self-doubt talking, not fact.

cards.prompt: I felt disappointed about the rejection, and then applied again elsewhere.
cards.explanation: Feeling disappointment and still continuing to try is a sign of a realistic, resilient self-view.

cards.prompt: One rejection was enough to make me stop trying entirely.
cards.explanation: Letting a single rejection stop all future effort is a self-doubt pattern generalizing far beyond the evidence.

cards.prompt: I took the rejection hard for a day or two, but then I got back to job searching.
cards.explanation: Taking a hit and then getting back up is realistic processing — self-doubt is when the hit becomes the whole story you tell about yourself.

cards.prompt: I have things I'd like to improve about myself, and I'm working on a couple of them.
cards.explanation: Identifying specific things to work on is a balanced, realistic form of self-awareness.

cards.prompt: I can't think of a single thing I like about myself.
cards.explanation: A total blank when trying to find anything positive is a strong sign of self-doubt distorting the picture.

cards.prompt: I notice my flaws, but I also notice things I'm good at.
cards.explanation: Holding both flaws and strengths at once is what a realistic self-view actually looks like.

cards.prompt: I only ever notice what's wrong with me, never what's working.
cards.explanation: A one-sided focus that only ever finds fault is self-doubt filtering out anything positive.

cards.prompt: I was self-critical about something today, but a friend pointed out I was being harsh, and I could actually see it.
cards.explanation: Being able to recognize you were being harsh, once it's pointed out, is a sign of a realistic self-view underneath — self-doubt usually resists that reframe entirely.

cards.prompt: I'm not sure how things will turn out, but I feel capable of handling whatever comes.
cards.explanation: Trusting your ability to handle uncertainty, even without knowing the outcome, is a realistic, steady mindset.

cards.prompt: I'm convinced things will go badly no matter what I do.
cards.explanation: A blanket certainty of bad outcomes regardless of your actions is self-doubt, not a real prediction.

cards.prompt: I have goals I'm working toward, even if the path isn't fully clear yet.
cards.explanation: Working toward goals despite an unclear path is a sign of realistic, grounded confidence.

cards.prompt: I've stopped setting goals because I'm sure I'll just fail at them anyway.
cards.explanation: Giving up on goals in advance, from a certainty of failure, is self-doubt shutting down possibility.

cards.prompt: I'm uncertain about a big decision coming up, but I trust I'll figure it out as I go, like I usually do.
cards.explanation: Trusting your own track record, even amid uncertainty, is the essence of a realistic self-check — self-doubt discounts your track record entirely.
